lines.note: Tria completes Induſ-tria from f294, now further explained as a great stratagem. Jucqeiga tçu-qita begins an example about exhausting all resources.
Tçu-qita completes the verb: all remedy and ingenuity have run out. This is running text, not the repeated catchword from the preceding page.
Juku suru means reaching ripeness or maturity. The initial is capital I; the Portuguese word ma-duro continues on the next row.
Completes maduro and begins conomiga jucuxita, the fruit has ripened. A frui- starts the Portuguese translation across another physical division.
Ta completes fruita: the fruit is now ripe. The visible grave accent in eſtà is retained.
Jukubaku is ripe grain, paraphrased as jucuxita mugui. The Portuguese specifies wheat or barley rather than treating mugui as exclusively one crop.

runs.text: da madura, ou que està de vez. S.

lines.note: Completes ceua-da and the ripeness explanation, with S. marking written usage. The physical continuation is indented. The second pass resolves the visibly tall ſ/t ligature here as long ſ.
Jukuden denotes good cultivated lowland or good soil. Varzea is kept as the printed Portuguese term.
Jukugi similarly denotes good or fertile land. It remains a separate headword from jukuden.

runs.text: Duas, ou mais letras, ou palauras que

lines.note: Jukugo is explained as two or more written characters or words functioning together. The definition continues with their combined sense and literary use.

runs.text: juntas tem o meſmo ſentido, & ſe vſão na Chi

lines.note: The characters or words together have a shared meaning and are used in China. There is a visible separation in juntas tem. The final Chi is capitalized and continues as na below, without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: na, & em Iapão elegantemente, como ſentẽça.

lines.note: Completes China, adds Japan, and describes elegant use like a maxim or sentence. The initial of Iapão is capital I, not lowercase l.

Jukumen denotes deep sleep, explained by fucǒ nemuru. The damaged m has faint left-side traces and can resemble n; the supplied NINJAL index corroborates the lexical identification after visual reading. The baseline’s internal space is retained, and the small mark over o is read as a caron. Lexical-aid attribution: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (supplied page subset).
Jukuqua is mature fruit, explicitly jucuxita conomi. Its final qua is retained as the historical spelling.
A second jukuqua is a ripe melon, jucuxita vri. The narrower fruit sense is not merged with the preceding general entry.
Jukushi denotes very ripe persimmons, described in the gloss as Japanese figs. The Portuguese comparison is preserved rather than replaced in the canonical text.
Jukusho is a long-inhabited residence, suminaretaru tocoro. The OCR’s initial long s is corrected to the visible capital I.

runs.text: em que ſe habitou muito tempo. Vt,

lines.note: The dwelling is one occupied for a long time. Jucuxo starts the ensuing saying about attachment to such a place.
Bǒjigataxi expresses difficulty in forgetting: one does not easily forget a familiar residence. The Portuguese explains this directly.

runs.text: do lugar onde morou muito tempo.

lines.note: Completes the saying as the place where one lived for a long time. This closes the residence entry before the next headword.
The garment entry is printed Iucufu and explained as what a Confucian scholar wears. Its consonant order is retained rather than silently changed to a more familiar modern form.

runs.text: veſtido de philoſophos moraes q̃ ha na China.

lines.note: Completes the description as the dress of moral philosophers in China. Philoſophos is one printed word, not the OCR’s philoſo phos.
Another Iucufu denotes life and prosperity, inochi ſaiuai. Despite sharing the printed headword with the garment entry, it has a distinct meaning.
Completes proſperidade and adds the goods or blessings of this life. The abbreviated bẽs and historical desta are preserved. The second pass resolves the visibly tall ſ/t ligature here as long ſ.

Iufiô is identified by vyekino kozue, the tips of a tree’s small branches. The uncommon headword is retained graphically; its meaning comes from the explicit bilingual gloss rather than an imposed modern reading.
Das aruores completes the branch-tip explanation. This short continuation precedes a separate religious headword.
Juhoo is receiving a law or teaching, noriuo vquru. A narrow but visible word space separates Receber from ley.
Jugaku is study, equated with gacumon suru. The example begins Iu-gacuno fito; the previously omitted capital I is visible after the paragraph mark.
Completes jugacuno fito, a student or students. The Portuguese uses the plural Estudantes. The second pass resolves the visibly tall ſ/t ligature here as long ſ.
Jugan is equated with jukon, friendship. Fito begins the example involving friendship with another person.
Fito ni jugan suru completes the example, being someone’s friend. The particle ni belongs to the preceding fito across the line break.
Jugi means receiving and keeping something, vqetamotçu. Its initial is capital I rather than long ſ.
Buppoo wo jugi suru illustrates receiving and keeping Buddhist law. Vt is italic as in the surrounding explanatory type.
Completes the law of the Fotoques and keeping it. Fotoques is a single Japanese-derived term embedded in Portuguese, not OCR Foto ques.

runs.text: Iugô. i, Ien acuno gôuo vquru.

lines.note: Jugoo concerns receiving the consequences of good and bad deeds. Ien acuno gôuo vquru is the Japanese explanation; initial I in Ien carries its historical consonantal value.

runs.text: o pago dos bens, ou males que hum fez.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the idea as payment or recompense for good or evil someone has done. The canonical wording is not replaced by modern doctrinal terminology.
Juugoraku denotes fifteen vessels in the medical account. The example juxtaposes twelve and fifteen channels; the initial I corrects OCR F.
Racu completes the Japanese phrase, followed by twelve and fifteen bodily vessels. The printed veas is retained rather than equated mechanically with modern anatomical veins.
The relative clause says these are the vessels discussed by physicians. This qualification locates the preceding numbers within a historical medical description.

runs.text: Iugue. Vyeqino xita. i, Qino moto.

lines.note: Juge means the base or underside of a tree, vyeqino xita and qino moto. Pè begins the Portuguese phrase completed below.
Completes the foot of the tree, then gives juge xeqixǒ, juxtaposing the tree’s base and the top of a stone. The Portuguese explanation follows.

runs.text: pè da aruore, ou ſobre a pedra.

lines.note: The example means being at a tree’s foot or on a stone. The two locations are alternatives in the gloss, not a single physical structure.

runs.text: Vinda de peßoa nobre a al-

lines.note: Jugyo is an honoured person’s arrival at a house, paraphrased as von iri. The divided al-gũa continues on the following row.
Completes algũa caſa, some house. The row closes the visit entry before the ox-picture entry.
Juugyuu no zzu names a set of painted ox figures. The first long-u mark was mistaken for n by OCR; both marked u vowels are retained from the scan.

runs.text: ſobre que os Ienxùs dão certos pontos de me-

lines.note: The figures furnish meditation topics for the Ienxùs, Zen religious. The initial of the embedded sect-name is read as I rather than OCR t; the grave on u is retained.
Ditaçoẽs completes meditaçoẽs. The tilde is printed over e in this occurrence and is not moved to match modern meditações.
Juin is tree shade, qino cague. The headword has a visible internal space, Iu in; Iit- begins the quotation’s word for sun and moon.
Iit-guet banbutuo teraſuto iyedomo says that although sun and moon illuminate all things, tree shade behaves differently. The object particle is attached to final t in banbutuo.

The shade does not receive light, completing the Japanese quotation. Xix. is a citation label; the Portuguese translation begins with sun and moon. The second pass resolves the visibly tall ſ/t ligature here as long ſ.

runs.text: a lũa fere todas as couſas com a ſua luz, toda

lines.note: Continues the Portuguese statement that the sun and moon strike all things with their light. Toda begins the contrastive expression continued below.

runs.text: via aſombra daruore não recebe luz.

lines.note: Toda via introduces the exception: tree shade receives no light. The joined aſombra and daruore are retained as printed, not normalized.
Juiqi is the limit of life, inochino ſacai. The initial is capital I rather than lowercase i.

runs.text: Chegar a hora da morte. S.

lines.note: Juiqini itaru means reaching the hour of death. The final S. marks the example as written usage.
Juit means filling and overflowing, michi afururu. Its final checked t is preserved without adding a syllable.

runs.text: Couſa fraca, ou manſa. S. Vt,

lines.note: Juujaku describes weakness or gentleness. The example begins Iǔ-jacu and contrasts these qualities with strength and severity.
Completes juujaku and adds cǒqiǒ. The Portuguese begins the opposition of frailty and softness to firmness and severity.
Completes the contrast with strength and severity. These nouns explain cǒqiǒ rather than adding a new entry.
Juuzen is the ten virtues, touono jen. The Portuguese defines them by opposition to the ten evils already listed.

runs.text: postas aos dez peccados de que ſe falou a cima.

lines.note: Completes contrapostas and refers back to the previously discussed ten sins. The spaced a cima is preserved. The second pass resolves the visibly tall ſ/t ligature here as long ſ.
The cross-reference points to juu aku, followed by an example of practising the ten virtues. Its printed internal spacing differs from the earlier headword and is retained.

runs.text: xercitar as dez virtudes. S. ¶ Item, Dig-

lines.note: Completes exercitar as dez virtudes and adds a second meaning beginning dignidade. The final S. belongs to the virtue usage before Item.
Nidade real completes dignidade real, royal dignity. This short row supplies a separate sense under the same printed headword.
Juujin is a follower or servant, xitagǒ fito. The Portuguese describes a servant or person of service.
Seruiço completes the servant definition. It is not connected to the maxim in the next entry.
Juujo means reaching the utmost height. The initial I and caroned u are visible and replace the OCR’s isolated ù; the conditional ſure-ba is divided.
The maxim says that reaching the summit necessarily leads to collapse. The scan supports two z letters in cuzzuru; Xix. is a citation label, not Japanese running text.

runs.text: ſummo logo vem a queda, ou destruição: vſa-

lines.note: The Portuguese translation gives a fall or destruction immediately after reaching the top. Its colon introduces the explanation of how the saying is used. The second pass resolves the visibly tall ſ/t ligature here as long ſ.

runs.text: ſe a cerca dos que chegarão a grandes honras,

lines.note: The saying applies to people who attained great honours. The clause is continued, not a new headword.
And they then fall: this completes the explanation of the maxim. The short row is retained as its own physical line.
Juuman is complete fullness, michi miteru. The Portuguese a-bundante is physically divided after a. The second pass resolves the visibly tall ſ/t ligature here as long ſ.
Completes abundance, then gives yorocobi juuman, fullness of joy. Sũma begins the corresponding Portuguese phrase.
Completes supreme joy or complete contentment. The emotional example illustrates fullness figuratively rather than the filling of a container.
Jumat is foam, equated with aua. The example compares the body to foam; the headword begins with capital I, not OCR long ſ.

The body is like foam and the mind or spirit like wind. Cajeno gotoxi preserves the historical voiced consonant spelling rather than replacing it with modern kazeno. The second pass resolves the visibly tall ſ/t ligature here as long ſ.

runs.text: corpo he como hũa eſcuma que logo ſe apaga,

lines.note: The Portuguese expands the foam comparison as something that disappears immediately. Its relative clause continues into the wind comparison.

runs.text: & o ſpiritu como vento quo logo paßa. Bup.

lines.note: The spirit is compared to passing wind, with Bup. marking Buddhist usage. Printed quo is retained despite the expected Portuguese que; the final paßa uses the visible ligature.
Juumen, literally ten faces, is explained as ten different facial gestures or expressions. The worn initial is capital I, not lowercase l.

runs.text: caretas que hum faz differentes no rosto.

lines.note: The Portuguese specifies different faces or grimaces made with one’s own face. Rosto is retained in its printed historical typography. The second pass resolves the visibly tall ſ/t ligature here as long ſ.
Jumyoo is life, equated directly with inochi. The entry is a complete single-row definition.
Jumoku is a tree, vyeqi. The compiler first gives the common restricted sense of a fruit tree, beginning the qualification cor-re no vulgo.

runs.text: re no vulgo. Porem o proprio ſentido he qual-

lines.note: Completes the statement about common usage and contrasts it with the proper or broader sense. Qual- continues into the next row.
Quer aruore completes qualquer aruore, any tree. This explicit contrast prevents narrowing the whole entry to fruit trees.
Juumonji denotes the character meaning ten. The initial is a roman I, not the OCR’s italic H; a second cross-shaped sense follows.
Adds the form of a cross, then begins an example of moving vertically and horizontally in a cross pattern. Jǔmon-jini is physically divided.
Completes the adverbial cross-pattern expression and describes breaking through enemies. The Portuguese begins the corresponding military example.

runs.text: inimigos por todas as quatro partes.

lines.note: The translation specifies breaking through enemies in all four directions. This is an application of the cross shape, not a separate entry.
Junboku is glossed as rice, with Vzzurame as its Japanese equivalent. The two z shapes are preserved from the crop rather than simplifying the historical form.
Jundoo is illustrated by jundoo ganrei, covering all kinds of small creatures. The worn initial is capital I rather than long ſ.
Bichos completes the general-creatures gloss. This short continuation belongs to the first jundoo entry.
A second jundoo denotes the proper path or direct road. The identical printed form is retained as a separate entry with a different gloss.
Completes the route as leading to some place. Algũa bears its tilde over u in this occurrence.

runs.text: O inuocar dez vezes o nome de A-

lines.note: Juunen is invoking Amida’s name ten times. The worn headword is read with a circumflex on u, unlike the caron in the following example; the capital I and independent-entry placement are restored.
Mida completes Amida, followed by juunen wo sazzuquru. Pro- begins the Portuguese explanation, which continues on f296 and is anticipated by the catchword.
